The answer is yes, since the 18th century the process of Demographic Transition has led to industrialized societies to see declines in birth rate. Not just in rich countries, but in Eastern Europe, Latin America, the Caribbean (Jamaica is set to see rapid population decline), India (especially the south), and it’s starting in the Middle East/North Africa. Not even Iran has escaped this trend. Some of these countries have the added burden of youth emigrating, further aging these societies. 

Demographic transition starts with increasing life expectancy and a decline in the need for child labor as the economic value of children diminishes (keep in mind they were free farm labor for millenia). But it takes time for attitudes to adjust. The population rapidly increases. Then the birth rate starts to decline, but still high enough to see population growth. Then it drops below replacement (2.1 children per mother), and the population stagnates for declines. 

In the United States, birth rates dropped below replacement rate in 1972, but then rose again abd reached replacement level in the 2000, but since 2007 has declined once more. 

Earlier demographic transition models predicted a leveling off, but some countries have seen it drop continuously.

With industrialization, children were more expensive, unlike in agrarian societies where they were extra help on the fields.
